#6753. What the “Ferritin Face” Trend Says About the Future of Beauty

Dark circles? A dull, washed-out complexion? Hair that’s seemingly shedding more than usual, or nails that break at the slightest touch? According to a growing corner of TikTok, the culprit could be your ferritin levels. Dubbed ‘ferritin face’, the viral new term links a collection of visible beauty changes to low ferritin, the protein responsible for storing iron in the body.

From ‘cortisol face’, the TikTok shorthand for facial puffiness allegedly linked to elevated stress, to the weight loss-adjacent ‘Ozempic face’, social media is now a hotbed for decoding what the body might be telling us in the mirror. So far, #FerritinFace has amassed more than 16 million views on TikTok, with videos of users attempting to identify the signs in their own appearance, offering advice on everything from supplements to traditional Chinese medicine, and even facial mapping. Since October, Google searches have been up 5,000% in the UK alone.

However, the conversation has also attracted a wave of caution from health professionals, warning against drawing medical conclusions from skin-deep assumptions.

“Ferritin is the protein that stores iron in your body, so a blood ferritin level is essentially a snapshot of your iron reserves — your ‘tank’ rather than just the iron circulating in your blood at that moment,” explains Dr. Lamia Zafrani, a recognized leader in women’s health. Iron plays a crucial role in oxygen transport, energy production, and healthy hair and nails, meaning depleted reserves can have implications for how we look and feel. Yet, she stresses that if someone suspects they might have it, “the first step is to see your GP and specifically ask for a ferritin test alongside a full blood count.”

Still, the trend points to a broader shift in how consumers engage with beauty: moving away from simply treating what they see in the mirror with topical or superficial solutions, and toward understanding the potential causation beneath the skin. Where once dark circles might have prompted a new eye cream, there is now a growing appetite to investigate the why — from nutrition and hormones, to gut health and cellular aging.

For the beauty industry, it indicates a future in which skincare sits alongside diagnostics, supplements and personalized wellness services, with a growing number of players looking to meet that demand. But how much can our appearance really reveal about our internal health? Can we really diagnose imbalances like low ferritin by simply looking at ourselves? And as consumers become more interested in finding the cause rather than combatting the symptom, who will stand to benefit from a growing health-led approach to beauty?

“Much like Ozempic face, ferritin face is another example of a social media trend prescribing beauty standards and boxing specific symptoms or effects into a ‘look’,” says Lisa Payne, head of beauty at Stylus. There is a more constructive side to the conversation, though. While trends like these can shift perceptions of beauty and create new aesthetic anxieties, Payne argues that ferritin face also encourages consumers to approach beauty more holistically.

“I grew up in Korea, where it’s standard to believe that the face reflects what is happening inside the body; it’s been read as a signal for generations,” says Mina Lee, founder and creative director of her eponymous Chelsea facial studio. “So ferritin face strikes me not as a discovery, but as an old instinct finding a new vocabulary. I think the vocabulary is now clinical: not just ‘I look tired’, but inflammation, ferritin, thyroid.”

Lee’s own approach takes a similarly inside-out view of skin, although she is careful not to reduce it to any one marker or diagnosis. “My approach, and what we do at the studio, has never been just about what the eye can see. Before I touch someone’s face, I want to know what they have been eating, how their digestion is, what is keeping them awake, and what’s on their mind,” she adds. “Much of what appears on the skin begins somewhere in that conversation.”

Mina Lee, founder and creative director of her eponymous Chelsea facial studio.

Now, she is seeing this approach play out beyond Korea, especially in the West. “It’s partly because access to [health] tests and [wellness tracking] wearables are providing people with metrics they’ve never had. I suspect that it’s also due to fatigue with surface-level fixes, encouraging the idea to look inward,” Lee says. We’re also spending more time than ever looking at ourselves, meaning the more familiar we become with our own reflections, the more likely we are to notice — and try to explain — every change. “We look at our own faces more than any generation before us, be it on video calls, in a front-facing camera, all day. Becoming more aware of and noticing our faces is expected.”

Still, experts are cautious of consumers overanalyzing and self-diagnosing, as the popularity of these terms rises. “Although all the external indications associated with ferritin face can be associated with low iron or ferritin levels, they are also quite general and could be attributed to a multitude of other health conditions,” says Pupinder Ghatora, pharmacist and co-founder of supplement brand Ingenious. Dark circles, dull skin and a tired complexion can be a result of many other causes, including genetics, hormonal changes, dehydration, stress, and poor sleep. “Ferritin face is not a recognized medical diagnosis, and you cannot determine someone’s iron levels by looking at them. If someone is experiencing persistent fatigue, unusual hair loss, paler skin or other symptoms that concern them, they should speak to a healthcare professional rather than trying to diagnose themselves through social media.”

“It’s also important to understand why someone may be iron deficient, rather than simply trying to correct the numbers,” cautions Xenia Mitsiou, senior registered nurse and advanced aesthetic practitioner at the Knightsbridge-based HVN longevity clinic. “Iron supplements can be very helpful when needed, but taking them without establishing whether there is a deficiency can cause side effects and, in excess, toxicity. It can also mean that an underlying cause is missed.”

Lee is supportive of the thinking behind the trend, but also cautions against drawing conclusions from appearance alone. “Of course, I’m a big advocate for the underlying principle and question being asked. People are right to be viewing with a lens that looks deeper than just surface level, and that belief has sat at the heart of my work for 20 years,” she says. If consumers are concerned, Lee recommends treating what you see as a question, not a conclusion. “I’d suggest looking at patterns over weeks rather than a single photograph, or while examining yourself at eleven at night in bad light. At the same time, equally consider whether your daily habits and choices are caring ones.”

Payne predicts that the rise of trends like ferritin face will accelerate demand for a more personalized approach to beauty, with brands using scans and tests to make more tailored product recommendations. “Examples where brands present companion products — such as supplements to take alongside a topical product — will resonate especially,” she says.

Some of the industry’s biggest players are already moving in this direction. In March, Lancôme launched Cell BioPrint, a diagnostic device developed by parent company L’Oréal that uses a cheek swab, facial imaging, and protein biomarker analysis to assess skin biology and provide personalized recommendations. Meanwhile, Nestlé Health Science has introduced Solgar Smart Mirror, an AI-powered facial scanning tool that offers tailored wellness insights.

Associated technology is beginning to attract interest beyond the beauty counter. “Interestingly, Japanese scientists are already investigating whether AI could identify signs of anemia [a lower-than-normal red blood cell count] by analyzing the inside of our lower eyelids,” says Dor Bukobza, founder of London’s Waldor Clinic, which specializes in South Korean and Japanese technology. He references a study published in July 2026, involving 225 participants, which explores how AI could analyze images of the inner eyelid to estimate haemoglobin levels (a protein that relies on iron to carry oxygen around the body) and identify potential signs of anemia.

The Waldor Clinic, located in London, specializes in South Korean and Japanese technology.

“The results are fascinating,” Bukobza says, “because they suggest that certain areas around our eyes may offer information about our internal health that isn’t apparent from simply looking at someone’s face.” There are important caveats, however. “The research is at an early stage, and detecting anemia is very different from measuring ferritin.” Indeed, haemoglobin measures the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, while ferritin measures the iron stored in the body. Ferritin levels can fall before haemoglobin levels, meaning someone can have iron deficiency without yet developing anemia.

The appetite for beauty-from-within products — from functional beverages that support gut health like Poppi, to drinkable skincare like Kylie Jenner’s K20 electrolyte brand — can be seen in their continuous rollout. According to Euromonitor International, 20% of dietary supplements launched globally since the second half of 2024 carry some form of beauty claim. Beauty-positioned supplements also grew by 6% in real terms in 2025, compared with 2% growth across the wider consumer health market.

“There has been a boom in supplement interest as more people become aware of what is happening inside the body, rather than just trying to conceal or treat what they see on the outside,” says Ingenious’s Ghatora. “Consumers are increasingly looking beyond topical products and thinking about how their health, nutrition, and lifestyle influence their appearance.”

For Ghatora, the next challenge is ensuring that the products entering this space are backed by credible science. “Consumers are becoming more ingredient-aware, and they want to understand what they are taking, why they are taking it, and whether there is evidence behind the claims,” he says. “Brands that prioritize transparency, appropriate dosages, and clinically supported ingredients will be better placed to build long-term trust than those relying on viral trends or exaggerated promises.”

There is also a risk that greater awareness encourages consumers to self-diagnose and supplement unnecessarily. “My biggest concern is when awareness turns into self-diagnosis and then unnecessary supplementation. Iron is essential, but taking additional iron when it is not needed can cause side effects and can even be harmful. It is also important to identify why someone’s iron levels are low rather than simply trying to correct the number,” Ghatora adds.

Despite the opportunities and risks, for Lee, it all signals a positive development in the kinds of questions consumers are asking. “What I do find hopeful is that the question itself has shifted from ‘what can I put on this?’ to ‘what is this telling me?’ It moves people from correcting themselves to caring for themselves,” she says. That doesn’t mean turning every change in appearance into a problem to solve, though. “Remember, your face is also allowed to simply be a face. Sometimes, tiredness is tiredness, and the honest advice is rest rather than a test result or a new product.”

#6751. Medallion Belts Are Everywhere

Consider it a chicer take on the old Western belt.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

If the runways are any indication, we’ve all been loving a good, impactful belt. Marc Jacobs loaded models up with 2008-coded chain belts at his most recent show, while McQueen wrapped black leather creations around the waist, which also snaked up to the neck like collar harnesses. Celine presented hulking supersize belts that cemented creative director Michael Rider’s dedication to standout accessorizing for spring/summer 2027. Yet at the center of it all lives the medallion belt. Consider it the most wearable version of the statement belt trend.

The look is an easy way to accessorize instantly. Medallion belts act as a kind of jewelry in this case, with their chunky hardware leading the way. Whether paired with jeans and a T-shirt or slung over a little black dress, they’re both practical and slightly whimsical. Both Dior and Celine have put an emphasis on the medallion silhouette, with chic, polished medal belt buckles engraved with designer logos.

Gilded in gold tones and attached to luscious leather, the designer medallions act as modern cartouches, proudly displaying the brand’s name like a badge. It’s definitely a modern take on logomania. Dior has also used the same medallion design seen on its belts in its beauty products, proving there’s always a desire for cute, shiny things. If the shape feels inherently Marie Antoinette-ified, it’s intentional. Its inspiration draws from the 18th-century Rococo aesthetic of Dior’s couture salons.

Chloé too has released a medallion belt. While it’s less logo-driven, it has all the major hallmarks that make the look both elevated and impactful. Four golden, gleaming horse heads surround a talismanic design. The horse motif is a clear nod to the bohemian style that is closely tied to the fashion house’s history. It also heavily relates to the lineage of the medallion belt itself, which has been around for centuries (from ancient Rome’s military uniforms and beyond) but thrived during the 1970s when Western wear reached a peak obsession. The rounded shapes of modern medallion belts of today also reference the original Native American concho belts, which originated in the American Southwest during the late 1860s and blended Spanish-Mexican aesthetics.

What sets the medallion belt apart from some of the other trending belts of the moment is its inherent ease and practicality. Some brands are even taking things a step further. For Givenchy’s spring/summer 2027 show, creative director Sarah Burton gave the medallion belt a makeover by turning the gilded emblem into a usable compact mirror. These days, the medallion belt is a real rarity in fashion: it’s an opulent staple that’s actually practical, too.

Valentino Garavani Butterfly-Buckle Leather Belt

#6750. Can Hermès Make a Watch as Iconic as the Birkin?

I arrived in Miami expecting to see the latest watches from Hermès. But as representatives of the historic Parisian luxury house led a group of us through the Rubell Museum, there was no sign of the timepieces. After passing through rooms showcasing Basquiat, Keith Haring, and Anselm Kiefer on the walls, we came into a room that looked more like an art classroom than a luxury-watch launch. Instead of being shown new editions of the H08, which Hermès has been slowly sculpting into an icon, I was handed a paintbrush.

Present in the room was Cuban American artist José Parlá, along with tables covered in paint, brushes, and scraps of paper torn from street advertisements. On the walls hung canvases Parlá had already begun and which would serve as the starting point for our own creations.

Delighted by the surprise arts-and-crafts, I happily donned my apron. Later that day, Hermès would unveil two new versions of its distinctive H08, the sporty model it debuted in 2021 and has been carefully building up. The latest pair introduced into the catalog both feature ceramic bezels, one in blue and another in white. They share a shimmering fiberglass case coated in aluminum that gives the watch the look of a tumultuous, gray sea.

When it was first released, the H08 garnered immediate praise from the collector community and broader market. Such rave reviews out of the gate are nearly unheard of for a completely new collection. The H08 is defined by its vaguely rectangular case with soft, sloping edges; the straight lines of the watch are contrasted by a round concentric dial. Paired with colorful, complementary rubber straps or the occasional bracelet, the H08 is a collection clearly intended for an active lifestyle without veering into the realm of the tool watch.

Hermès is a Goliath in the luxury world with a massive multibillion-dollar business across leather goods, handbags, and silk scarves. But amid all of its exceptional offerings, watches were never a primary focus; they were something one might add in while buying a Birkin. The H08 is an opportunity for Hermès, a maker of icons, to establish one in a category where it’s still establishing its reputation.

Inside the museum workroom, I set about the task of customizing my canvas. I chose one reminiscent of a rich, red sunset. I sorted through the sheets of torn paper that resembled craggy mountaintops, glued them down, and began to paint. I felt like I was transported back to my childhood art classes.

I realized that this was not simply an activity to fill the time but was actually a sophisticated metaphor for how Hermès views the creative process itself, especially as it applies to the development of pieces like the new H08s. The work is collaborative, iterative, and builds on the concept of what came before to create something new. The base is familiar enough to collectors at this point, but new colors and approaches round out a growing army of H08s so everyone can choose their flavor.

“We understood that our way to make this line grow would be to animate it and go deeper into materials,” Laurent Dordet, CEO of La Montre Hermès, the house’s Swiss watchmaking subsidiary. “It’s part of the playground of H08.” While the H08 already comes in a host of colors and accents, from bright teals and oranges to blues, greens, and yellows, the new bright blue and white variants bring a fresh, almost resortwear vibe to the collection.

H08 has given Hermès a foundation to build its limitless creativity on top of. The fundamental design hasn’t changed at all, but Hermès has continuously renewed it through new colors and materials. Hermès has played with satin brushing, DLC or colored PVD-coated titanium, and carbon composites coated with graphene powder. There are also skeletonized versions of the watch as well as ones with a chronograph (or a stopwatch function). As the H08 was always intended to be the brand’s far-reaching sport offering, opening up Hermès to new clients and lifestyle applications, the collection quickly became the vehicle for such innovation.

But even if Hermès isn’t primarily a watch brand, the house’s world-class artisans never passed off second-rate design. And the playfulness that pervades the house is essential to the watches too. “That’s what our clients expect from us. Hermès is obsessed with making a beautiful object that will bring comfort and pleasure to its owner,” Dordet says. “We are not obsessed with having something fun or playful every time. It's a balance between style, elegance, sobriety, subtlety, colors.”

Later that evening, at Hermès’s Miami Design District boutique, I encountered another expression of the company’s creative imagination: a smaller version of Jean-Simon Roch’s kinetic sculpture Mysterious Mechanics, which had appeared at the industry’s flagship trade show Watches and Wonders earlier in the year. Its elaborate system of ropes, pulleys, and moving frames was a theatrical interpretation of mechanical timekeeping, part of the broader cabinet of curiosities that informs Hermès’s creative universe.

As I stood before Mysterious Mechanics, I realized it would be all too easy for Hermès to tap into this same type of whimsy to create an H08 that was loud or multicolored in some obvious embodiment of abstract art. But that just isn’t how Hermès works. The brand understands that a signature watch is forged over generations. Look at a model like the Rolex Submariner—one of its most valuable assets is that the base design is largely unchanged over 70 years. There’s a beautiful juxtaposition between the very serious, capital-L luxury done at the highest levels of capability and concept, and the fun-loving, whimsical approach to how Hermès creates. Perhaps that’s why the brand has endured for nearly 200 years. And also why the H08 may just be its next iconic creation.

#6748. The Fringe Pieces Fashion Insiders Are Wearing This Fall

Runways say this is the adornment of the season.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Fringe never really goes out of style. No matter the season, you can always expect to see the embellishment swaying from the arm of a suede jacket or dangling off a leather bag. So when it comes to trends around the design detail, it’s a mere matter of what form the fringe takes. Lately, fashion’s found itself in a fringe fixation, prompting the trim to move beyond the Western-inspired looks it’s best known for.

Fringe re-emerged on the scene last fall when spring/summer 2026 catwalks from Bottega Veneta, Givenchy, and Chanel showcased the adornment as playful ornamentation for skirts, bags, and even shoes. By the fall/winter 2026 season, others were beginning to chime in with their own takes. There were the boho-inspired bags from Etro, the romantic wispy dresses from Ulla Johnson, and restrained silhouettes from Altuzarra.

Whether you’re looking for a bold statement or a little wink of style, fringe remains a simple way to add flair to any outfit. And right now, there’s a fringed version of just about any wardrobe piece you could think of. Between the classic leather staples and newer avant-garde styles, you’ll find something for every style sensibility.

Do an online search for fringe jackets, and you’ll find no shortage of options to shop. Leather and suede remain tried-and-true materials for this style of outerwear—but now there’s also a plethora of other textiles to shop as well. Opt for Toteme’s viral scarf coat if you’re in the market for a new winter coat, or this tweed number from Etro if you’re looking for a polished piece you can wear to the office.

Nili Lotan Eloi Fringe-Trimmed Suede Jacket

Simon Miller Mabel Vegan Leather Fringe Jacket

If recent fall/winter 2026 runways from Givenchy and Proenza Schouler show us anything, it’s that fringe dresses are reaching new heights. The trim is an especially pretty touch to formalwear and event dresses, providing playful movement with every step to even the simplest silhouettes.

Cara Cara Troy Floral-Print Fringe-Trimmed Cotton-Blend Jersey Midi Dress

Ciebon Nella Asymmetric Fringe Midi Dress

Cult Gaia Noosha Fringed Silk Halterneck Maxi Dress

Just like dresses, fringe skirts are experiencing a similarly sophisticated evolution. Lately, the style has favored sleek satin fringe to create a distinct piece that will immediately elevate anything it’s paired with.

Bottega Veneta Fringed Knitted Silk Midi Skirt

Alaïa Tassle Fringed Asymmetric Wool-Gabardine Midi Skirt

Anna Sui Asymmetric Floral-Flock Fringe-Trimmed Crepe Midi Skirt

The sky’s the limit when it comes to fringe bags these days. There’s long fringe and short fringe. There’s standard leather and suede trim that adds a timeless flair, or more dramatic confections made of sequins, beads, or feathers. With beaded tassel bags on the rise, it makes sense that fringe would take similar cues for an eclectic flourish.

Fendi Croissant Fringed Calf Hair Shoulder Bag

Nili Lotan Asher Fringed-Trimmed Suede Shoulder Bag

After Givenchy debuted a pair of bold fringed mules as part of its spring/summer 2026 collection, fringe exploded onto shoes—heels in particular—in a big way. These Boudoir mules, as they came to be known, introduced a playful take on fringe footwear. Now it’s an ultra-luxe, fashion-forward style that’s perfect for those who never shy away from making a statement.

#6745. Why Are These Huge Arc’teryx Boots Suddenly Going Viral?

​Where were you during the Great Arc’teryx Jacket Phenomenon of 2022? If you’ve forgotten, the cult Canadian outdoors label went viral when young men on TikTok began filming themselves in the shower to demonstrate the hypnotic water-repelling ability of their Gore-Tex jackets. The attention only seemed to further cement Arc’teryx’s techy outerwear as an inescapable part of the menswear landscape. Now, the Vancouver brand appears to have another crossover hit on its hands: a hulking beast of a winter boot.

The Postour is a two-in-one design that combines a weatherproof outer boot with a removable insulated slipper tucked inside. In what the brand calls “full-boot mode,” the high collar cinches shut with a utility cord, sealing you off from the elements. The idea is that you can spend the day stomping through snow and slush, then shed the outer shell and lounge around in the slippers. Though it almost looks like a chalk bag sprouted a foot, the silhouette still carries the sleek, hyperfunctional minimalism the brand is known and loved for. The oddness of the design seems to be part of the appeal.

Naturally, it’s equipped with all the technical bells and whistles you’d expect from Arc’teryx: a gnarly Vibram Arctic Grip outsole, weatherproof Gore-Tex shell, and the label’s proprietary Coreloft insulation. Perhaps most covetably, there’s also a giant skeletal bird logo—known to diehards as the “deadbird”—on the side. The same logo has helped make the brand’s beanies a favorite of everyone from Timothée Chalamet to Frank Ocean.

Much like Arc’teryx’s Gore-Tex jackets before it, the Postour has become unmissable on the men’s side of the fashion algorithm. It’s a viral object of desire for a certain type of menswear guy fluent in microtrends. (This is hardly the first time we’ve seen a polarizing boot take over the algorithm, after all.) The is-this-ugly-or-cool discourse only adds fuel to the fire—and the fact that the boots resemble a sought-after design from Yeezy Season 8 certainly doesn’t hurt. TikTok and Instagram are chock full with videos of dudes excitedly unboxing their boots, blasting them with hoses, and customizing them with colored wax. As a result of all this digital buzz, the $300 boot has been drifting in and out of stock on the official Arc’teryx website. At one point last week, it was fully sold out; as of press time, only a couple of sizes remain in stock (though REI currently has a full size run).

Of course, winter footwear has its own pantheon of heavy hitters, from L.L.Bean’s iconic Bean Boot to Sorel’s felt-lined stompers and Timberland’s “40 Below” Super Boot. Whether the Postour will earn a place alongside those classics remains to be seen. For now, Arc’teryx has made the rare winter boot that’s as hyped up online as it is useful in a snowstorm. Good luck getting your hands on a pair.

#6744. These Perfumes Are So Irresistible, Strangers Will Stop You to Ask What You’re Wearing

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Finding your signature scent involves a lot of trial and error—and a tingling nose. Fragrance is powerful, and discovering a unique scent for daily or occasional wear can uplift your mood, evoke a memory, or make your presence known in any room before you even speak. Whether you’re hunting for a fragrance that feels distinctly you or building a perfume wardrobe to ensure you’re prepared for every event on your social calendar, shopping for perfume can feel overwhelming. One moment, everyone’s going for guava; the next, it’s all about sea salt.

Truth is, trends come and go. However, the journey to building a unique collection is about finding a fragrance that truly resonates—whether floral, gourmand, musky, or a distinct layered blend.

“Fragrance has the power to evoke memories of a person, a moment, an experience,” says DSM-Firmenich perfumer Bérénice Watteau. “We’ve all experienced it: walking down the street, catching a familiar scent on a stranger, and suddenly being brought back to someone we love or a beautiful memory shared with them. Perfume captures those fleeting feelings and makes them timeless.” Your scent should also feel like an extension of yourself, something that reflects your personality, style, and the way you want to be remembered. Don’t be afraid to layer a couple of scents for an irreplicable fragrance of your own creation.

As beauty editors, we’re lucky enough to spritz, sniff, and test hundreds of scents, so it takes a lot for one to impress us—that’s how you know the ones on the list below are extra special. We also consulted three experts and combed through numerous customer reviews to find 16 of the best perfumes for women that we can’t stop wearing.

Have you ever wondered what Kim Kardashian’s hair smells like? Well, here’s your answer. She uses the hair mist version of the Valaya Exclusif Eau de Parfum. The formula delivers a fresh, clean finish, anchored by a beautifully balanced blend of bergamot, mandarin, and white peach. Plus, the tassel-adorned bottle looks beautiful on display.

Smells like: A Kardashian’s hair (literally)

Key notes: Bergamot, mandarin, white peach

Customer review: “I’ve never been stopped so much by people asking for what fragrance I’m wearing! This is heavenly, and when you add with the Delina body oil it is really delightful and long lasting. Worth the try!”

Valentino gave their classic Born in Roma perfume a very delicious upgrade. The Donna Born in Roma Purple Melancholia Eau de Parfum is a deep purple color inspired by its top note of juicy plum accord. With jasmine and vanilla, the scent is floral, sensual, and warm.

ELLE editor review: “I was lucky enough to receive a sample of this scent a few weeks before its launch, and one spritz from the purple bottle was all it took to completely sell me. I’m a sucker for vanilla fragrances, and this one strikes the perfect balance: sweet but never overbearing, and indulgent without veering into anything overly sugary or childish. Since I started wearing it, the compliments haven’t stopped. While I felt undeniably cool wearing a scent no one else could get their hands on, I’m just as excited for everyone else to finally experience it.”—EAB

Starting with bright, surprising whiffs of jasmine, this perfume soon turns dark and seductive, with traces of coffee and cocoa. It’s a must-have for any wild night in or out.

Key notes: Almond, coffee, bergamot, lemon, jasmine, orange blossom, tonka bean, cacao, vanilla, sandalwood, patchouli, and cedar

Expert review: “ELLE editors made an entire TikTok about their favorite Good Girl fragrance. This one is perfect for your first date with a guy you met on Hinge. The aroma is warm, sweet, and sexy. I notice that on my friends who tend to run warmer, the sandalwood, vanilla, and orange blossom do a beautiful dance together.”—Danielle James, beauty expert

Baccarat Rouge 540 is arguably one of the most iconic and coveted perfumes of the 21st century. This perfume smells like pure luxury; the slightly sweet, floral scent settles into a spicy, earthy aroma as jasmine, cedar, and saffron take center stage.

Key notes: Jasmine, saffron, cedarwood, ambergris accord

ELLE editor review: “This perfume is a guaranteed conversation starter. The distinct smell either evokes the response of ‘Ahh, I love 540,’ amongst those who know it, or ‘What is that smell?!’ to those who are about to be introduced to the reigning queen of the perfume occult. The smell is intense and sultry without being overbearing.”—Emma Aerin Becker, associate beauty e-commerce writer

Perfumer Ben Gorham captured the essence of the color white by combining delicate florals, a woody base note, and a hint of musk; the scent makes you feel fresh, polished, and put-together, even in 90-degree weather.

Key notes: White rose, pink pepper, aldehyde, violet, neroli, peony, blonde woods, sandalwood, musk

Expert review: “Even though I think things like chocolate cake, bonfires, and the sea smell good, I don’t necessarily want to smell like them. But fresh linens? Sign me up! I bury my nose in my cotton sheets when I take them out of the dryer, and I bury my nose in my wrist when I wear this perfume.”—Carol Lee, beauty writer

There’s a reason you see this iconic bottle in practically every magazine you’ve ever opened. It’s a classic, and the fruity, floral ingredients never weigh down the luscious elegance of the ylang-ylang, jasmine, pear, and lily.

Key notes: Ylang-ylang, Damascus rose, jasmine

Expert review: “This warm floral somehow smells good on everyone who tries it, and it would be a fantastic gift for any occasion. I gave my roommates (who have very different tastes in fragrance) a bottle each for Christmas, and both of them were beyond delighted.”—CL

Many of Kilian’s scents evoke a boozy night at a sexy bar and make you feel and smell like the main character of any venue you walk into. On the Rocks expands on the sexy swing of the Angels’ Share collection—where Paradis opened with a berry burst, On the Rocks tickles your nose with the rinds of your favorite citruses: mandarin, lemon, grapefruit, and bitter orange. It’s not all fruits, though; the scent settles down into a swig of cognac, tonka bean, and sandalwood without ever overpowering its citrus notes.

Key notes: Italian lemon, grapefruit, bergamot, mandarin, bitter orange, tonka bean, cognac

ELLE editor review: “I feel like I should be in Italy every time I wear On the Rocks. The tangy notes, intermixed with the deeper, sexier ones we know Kilian for, elevate any outfit. I always get compliments around the office whenever I wear this.”—Nerisha Penrose

Think of all the best parts of summer—frozen citrus sorbets, sunny beach days, salty sea air—this perfume combines them into a sunny scent. Never-ending Summer is a perfume that keeps the summer vibes going, with notes of bitter orange, ginger, earl gray, and cedarwood.r

Key notes: Bitter orange, pepper duet, fresh ginger essence, earl grey accord, cardamom, vetiver, cedarwood, patchouli essence

ELLE editor review: “Just as its name suggests, this perfume truly is summer in a bottle. A few spritzes release notes of freshly peeled oranges and bright vetiver, instantly transporting me to a sun-drenched afternoon with an Aperol spritz in hand. As someone who’s perpetually chasing warm weather and carefree summer energy (I am a Leo, after all), this scent will be my go-to long past the season’s end—because sometimes you need a subtle reminder of your favorite time of year.” —EAB

Take a chance (pun intended) on this fruity and floral fragrance. Bursting with notes of jasmine, rose, and grapefruit, it’s slightly sweet yet refreshingly vibrant—prepare to field all of the compliments you’re bound to receive.

ELLE editor review: “Of all the perfumes I’ve tried over the years, Chanel's Chance has remained a constant in my lineup. It’s lighter and more modern than the brand’s iconic N°5 scent, yet is still just as effortlessly classic and long-lasting. In fact, I’ve found it to be such a universal crowd-pleaser that even an Uber driver once asked me what I was wearing.”—Sam Peters, contributor

The whole point of this perfume is that it smells like the best version of you. That is, a you that showers with expensive body wash and never sweats a drop. “I adore skin scents, and this one is musky, elegant, and intimate,” says Watteau. It creates a soft second-skin effect that feels personal and addictive.”

Expert review: “If you want to get into scent layering, Glossier You makes a great base scent. It’s familiar on its own, smells like the ‘you’ that just got out of the shower, but better. It’s bright, yet soft, and the perfect everyday scent for someone that doesn’t want anything too fussy.” —DJ

Ouds can be quite intimidating to delve into, especially if your palate has always leaned toward sweet, soft notes. Milky Oud from Kayali meets you in the middle, adding depth to a smoothie of strawberry cream, saffron, coffee, oud, and sandalwood.

Key notes: Oud, strawberry cream, incense, saffron

ELLE editor review: “Kayali’s Oudgasm collection marries the deep, darker aroma of the main ingredient with lighter notes to create everyday scents that turn heads in the best way. My favorite has always been Kayali’s Smoky Oud mixed with Vanilla Oud—Milky Oud is basically its golden child. Even though oud can be heavy in perfume, it softens in this juice with a second skin-like embrace.”—NP

Fame by Rabanne smells like a sexy night out in a beautiful tropical locale—fruity, spicy, and woody, with appearances from mango, incense, and sandalwood. “Gourmands aren’t usually my thing, but this is the only vanilla perfume I reach for over and over, especially for a night on the town,” says beauty writer Carol Lee. “Nerisha keeps a bottle by her desk in the office, and whenever she tries a scent we both can’t stand, she spritzes it all over as a delicious palate cleanser we both enjoy.”

Key notes: Mango, jasmine, incense, vanilla, sandalwood

ELLE editor review: “This sits at my desk and becomes an instant compliment magnet when I spray it on myself and wait for its aroma to permeate our office corner. It’s sexy and mysterious, but still inviting. While I don’t typically like to prescribe to day or night scents, this one is for the nocturnal lovers.”—NP

Buckle up tight because this fragrance takes you on a ride. The yin-yang scent composition unfurls a delicate composition of sensual citrus and florals, then comes the dip—warm almond milk, sandalwood, and white musk.

Key notes: Calypso orchid, mandarin, Bulgarian rose, almond milk, ylang ylang, iris, white musks, sandalwood

ELLE editor review: “As someone with over 100 fragrances, my signature scent changes daily. However, I almost always begin most of my scent layers with Yin Transformation, which bursts with creamy florals that feel like a balmy spring morning.”—NP

S.S.K Labs makes scent layering easier with its kits. Am-Edp is the brand's amber star, and this kit features perfume rollerball oils of myrrh and tonka bean, two notes that pair exceptionally well with amber. You can wear each on its own, or mix and match to form your own scent bubble.

Key notes: (Am) Amber, bergamot, pink pepper berry, orange blossom, musk; (Tonka) cardamom, cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger; (Myrrh) myrrh, lemongrass, cumin, amber, patchouli

ELLE editor review: “You can tell when amber is featured in a fragrance due to its warm, woody essence. Here, S.S.K Labs shows you exactly why the note is the go-to in olfactory compositions. Amber shines on its own, but the addition of tonka bean and myrrh elevates it to something sexier, spicier, and more elegant than anything I’ve smelled before.”—NP

Inspired by late nights partying in Paris, it’s no wonder Krigler’s Velvet Night 76 makes you want to get up and dance. With an intense floral-amber composition, the perfume opens with notes of bergamot and orange blossom that bloom into tuberose and jasmine, all before settling into the sensual warmth of vanilla and musk.

Smells Like: A popping Paris nightclub in the 1970s

Key notes: Bergamot, orange blossom, Italian tuberose, jasmine, vanilla, cedarwood, and musk.

ELLE editor review: “As a beauty writer, I sniff a lot of scents in my day-to-day. Some smell great, some are just fine, and others make me go, “wow.” Krigler Velvet Night 76 is the latter. One whiff transports you to Paris Fashion Week in the ’70s, with bustling streets and packed night clubs. It’s equally ideal for a sultry date night or a lively girls night out.”—EAB

If you love to mix and match your favorite scents, you’re in luck. 27 87 created their Lametta Eau De Parfum with layer-lovers in mind. Crafted around a patented musk, the subtle scent creates an intimate, second-skin effect that feels entirely personal. It works great as a stand-alone, but works even better with any of your favorite scents.

ELLE editor review: “If I’m being honest, I rarely layer my scents, However, in the name of journalism, I tested out the Lametta Eau De Parfum both on it’s own and paire with a few of my other go-tos. No matter what notes it touched, the result was always alluring—especially when balancing out sweet or floral scents.”—EAB

Joan Tanis is the national training and events director at Maison Francis Kurkdjian.

Tynan Sinks is a New York City-based beauty writer and the co-host of fragrance podcast Smell Ya Later.

Bérénice Watteau is a fine fragrance perfumer at DSM-Firmenich

What should you consider when choosing a perfume?

Understanding fragrance notes is one of the most effective ways to find your perfect scent. “Very similar to the fashion industry, there can be trends with fragrances as well,” Tanis says. “Choosing a fragrance isn’t always easy, but make the right choice by selecting one that reflects who you are and makes you feel good. My best advice is to let your personality, tastes, and age guide your choice.”

“The most important part of finding a fragrance is, of course, trying it on,” Tanis continues, adding that you can have multiple signature scents, rather than just one, for variety. “Nowadays, it is all about a collection of fragrances. Much like clothing, modern men and women desire a fragrance wardrobe, allowing them the freedom to choose what fragrance to wear daily.”

What is the difference between an eau de toilette and eau de parfum?

Many popular scents fall into these fragrance categories. The difference between the two lies in the concentration of perfume oil each contains, says Tanis. “Eau de toilettes (EDT) have a relatively lighter composition due to their low concentration of perfume oil— between five and 15 percent. On the other hand, Eau de parfums (EDP) have a higher concentration of perfume oils—typically between 12 and 18 percent—meaning they offer a significantly stronger scent that lasts between five and eight hours.”

Choosing between the two might come down to the specific occasion or the weather (i.e., you may lean towards a lighter scent for work and during the summer months, and a richer scent for nights out and during the winter). Check out our perfume terminology guide to learn more about fragrance terms.

Tanis suggests applying fragrance to the pulse points, where the skin is naturally warm, such as the wrists, neck, or inside the elbows. “This will allow the fragrance to warm up and reveal the perfume's sillage (trail) over time.”

#6742. My Packing Style: Creative Director Gabriella Khalil

When it comes to mastering the art of the travel wardrobe, it’s no surprise that our favorite fashion insiders also moonlight as packing pros. In My Packing Style, we tap some of the most well-traveled people we know for a peek inside their travel bags and vacation wardrobes to see how they take their style on the road. You’ve bookmarked the trip, you’ve screenshotted the outfits; now, a look at how it all comes together.

She founded the most stylish hotel in Grand Cayman and made an old office building in New York’s Financial District one of the city’s coolest addresses. Anything WSA creative director Gabriella Khalil turns her attention to becomes design gold—and that includes her travel wardrobe. Sculptural silver jewelry, leopard print accents, a floor-length (of course) black satin robe… the contents of her Rimowa are unsurprisingly glamorous, proving that a capsule closet needn’t be boring.

Her best tip? Packing in a palette, which, for an upcoming trip to Morocco, means earth tones. In her suitcase, rich caramel, chocolate brown, and burgundy velour get broken up by black and white staples and small glints of silver. “I love Marrakech because I always feel so inspired there,” says Khalil (who recently launched a Vette storefront, a running edit of everything she’s currently inspired by). “This trip, I’m also going to Tangier, which I’ve always wanted to visit. I’m so excited to discover the spectacular interiors and design there.”

Ahead of her holiday in the sun, we caught up with the design multi-hyphenate to quiz her on her top packing tips and best airport outfit formula—plus, why she’ll always travel with a tiny bit of animal print.

I typically pack the night before a trip. So it isn't a fully “in advance” pack, but it gives me a little buffer room, so I’m not panic-packing.

Unless there is a specific event I’m going to, I don't really pack in outfits—I pack in palettes and tones so everything is essentially mix and match. I do this across the board, even with bags!

I love to travel with brands that have really elevated pieces that can transition from day to night. The Park is one of my favorites: Their bodysuits are amazing with jeans or loose trousers during the day, and also can be fantastic in the evening with more elevated looks. I usually bring their long-sleeve and sleeveless pieces with me in both black and white.

Marrakshi Life has the best trench jackets—especially for traveling. They’re a super soft woven cotton and the shape is fantastic; it feels like loungewear but looks incredible. I also love Diotima because the pieces are beautifully detailed and super versatile, and I never travel without a pair of Ossou jeans.

My aluminum Rimowa carry-on. I just got a new travel tote by La Mama, and have been bringing that everywhere; I am obsessed with the matching pouch, too.

I typically wear a set (lately, I’ve been reaching for my Suzie Kondi velour set) with a nice, warm sweater or jacket layered on top and flats.

I bring compression socks with me on flights; my favorites are from Ricari. Also, peppermint tea.

Sweater or hoodie, always. I love my Ashlyn sweater because it’s cozy but structured—I can wear it on the plane but also on the trip itself.

I love sheet masks on vacation, especially Augustinus Bader and 111Skin face masks. I have also been really into using my Crown Affair hair towel when I shampoo my hair; I’m taking it with me when I travel.

I don't worry too much about things getting wrinkled because I feel it is inevitable. I always have an iron sent to my room when I unpack, and I try to get that sorted from the beginning so it makes life easier on the trip.

When it comes to jewelry, I am mainly a silver person. I tend to always stick with this when I travel (unless the pieces are two-toned metals, in which case I’ll make an exception). I also love to bring a very classic palette of bags with me—black, brown or burgundy—so they go with everything.

I have this really fantastic leopard print cardigan from Posse; I love it because I tend to wrap it around my shoulders for daytime and casual wear, but also it transitions so easily into night. I wear a lot of neutrals and it’s such a nice pop of print to all of my outfits, whether it’s a black dress or baggy jeans. I generally enjoy adding in pops of animal print when I travel; it instantly lifts a minimal palette.

I hate to admit it, but I am such an over-packer. I try so hard not to be, though!

Bring pieces that are super versatile—I have a leather jacket that I bring everywhere. I also try to bring pieces that make me feel super comfortable. This floral robe travels with me often.

#6740. Is 'The Only Living Pickpocket in New York' Immediately the Best Watch Movie Ever?

There are plenty of great movie watches: James Bond’s OG Rolex Submariner, Hans Gruber’s Cartier Tank, or even Hamilton’s made-for-Interstellar Murph. But there are very few great watch movies that dig into the myriad layers of meaning that compel real-world collectors. In that way, The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, which rolled out to theaters nationwide on October 30, is a timepiece-lover’s dream movie.

In the film, John Turturro gives an Oscar-buzzy performance as Harry Lehman, an aging New York hustler who has scraped by for decades without evolving with the world around him. He doesn’t have a phone, dances to vinyl records, pays at diners with cash, and rents Barbara Stanwych movies (“tapes,” he calls them) from the public library for his wife.

Naturally, Harry is drawn toward watches, both for his personal use as items to steal. Along the way of The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, there’s a cornucopia of watches and Easter eggs for collectors to appreciate: Director Noah Segan meticulously selected a watch to fit every character’s personality. It matters deeply to Segan whether a character is wearing a vintage Rolex Explorer 1016 or a modern Hublot; and the movie even gets deep into the inner workings of timepieces. A pawn shop owner, played by Steve Buscemi, deems a Patek Philippe “fugazi” and shows Harry the lack of jewels in the movement. Watches, as totems of an analog world imbued with personal and cultural history, aren’t just a detail, but a vital motif.

It’s clear that The Only Living Pickpocket in New York could only come from a writer-director embedded in the hobby themselves. And, in the future, Segan, along with the dealer Adam Golden who sourced the pieces for the film, plans to bring these essential watches to auction for charity. GQ talked with Segan about how he chose the film’s array of timepieces, the state of his own collection, and why he would make a terrible watch salesman.

Noah Segan: That’s a great question. I wouldn’t presume to jump on anybody else’s intent in terms of watches. I think obviously there are a lot of watches in movies that have become iconic. The first kind-of-nice watch I ever got myself was a TAG Heuer Monaco because I was such a huge fan of Steve McQueen and Le Mans. There are obviously a lot of watches that are worn. I don’t know how often they get woven into a story, but in our case, our story is not just about time, but time changing, time running out, and that in combination with very physical things, tactile things. We’ve got a pickpocket, he’s tactile. He touches you. The idea of a totem and an object representing those things started feeling very important to me, and watches do that for me.

I would probably be a very bad watch salesman simply because I would want to keep all my favorites. So I think maybe collector is where I should stay, but I’ve always been a very, for lack of a better term, sort of analog guy. I still shoot film with a camera. I spin records. I live in an old house. The classic car in the movie is my old car.

I was lucky enough to grow up in an environment that appreciates the marriage of engineering and art and history. To me, that Venn diagram is a solid circle when it comes to wristwatches. These are objects that can be beautiful, they can be sophisticated, they can represent personal historic endeavors and also the macrocosm of historic feats.

The idea of what a watch means when you think of it in terms of The Dirty Dozen [a WWII-era field watch for soldiers commissioned by Britain from 12 iconic Swiss watchmakers] being there for the military or [Paul] Newman’s Rolex Daytona and its engraving on the back that says, “Drive Carefully Me.” All of a sudden you’re talking about something bigger than us, a celebrity, probably one of the biggest celebrities of all time who did something absolutely crazy, which was not being a movie star, but being a race car driver. And yet his wife still said, “Drive Carefully Me.” So there’s the personal, there’s the promotional, there’s the macro and the micro, and they all are fascinating to me.

Well, a close friend of mine is Adam Golden, who has a company called Menta, is actually a watch dealer who deals in very specific, unique vintage watches of great provenance.

In considering the watch for Harry, I really wanted something that could bridge the gap between a very useful tool and something of value. And that watch represents a lot for people in that respect. There was a time when Harry was a younger man, and that would have been a really good, valuable, useful tool for him to have. It’s an understated watch. It’s easy to read. It can last through whatever you throw at it on the streets in New York.

And yet today it’s something of incredible value financially and also incredible value to him because it is his watch. It has been a tool for him. And I couldn’t think of a better example than that Rolex 1016 to represent that combination of factors. And so Adam found us that watch and loaned it to us to wear.

We built the other watches in the movie around [the 1016]. Giancarlo Esposito plays Detective Warren, [Harry’s] foil and mirror image. He both helps Harry and is keeping an eye on him. He wears a Tudor Tuxedo, which shares a lot of, as we say in the watch game, DNA with something like a Rolex Explorer. In fact, it was made by the same company, and yet it’s just a little different.

Steve [Buscemi’s character] wears a thin, gold Rolex Cellini on a gold bracelet that, again, is something that would have been definitely a luxury item back in the day and is an even bigger luxury item today, but still represents something of an older time. Meanwhile, the watch Dylan [a young mobster played by Will Price] has, the Hublot, is considered today to be a very flashy, modern watch. It has a modern chronograph movement. It’s made with very present-day materials. And in fact, he’s not wearing it. It’s stuffed into his gym bag, and he says, “I only wear that when I go out to flex,” because it doesn’t represent a daily tool to him.

All of these things were designed and lent to us by Adam Golden to talk about who these characters were and to reflect something about the characters in a world where the physical items and the physical representation matter.

I can walk you through all of it! We also had some interesting newer watches. We worked with an incredible team at Oris, a brand that’s been around forever, but remains really relevant. Victoria Morolis, who plays Eve, wears Oris. She’s a sort of younger hero in the movie and a punk computer hacker. She’s wearing the Oris Roberto Clemente, which is a watch that is very old-school in a lot of ways, but made with very 2026 technology.

She was wearing her very own gold Cartier tank. She said, “I am going to do this.” And we all said, “Of course you are, because you are the boss.”

Well, I have a personal feeling about that because I have a lot of knowledge of this stuff. This is my hobby, right? So to me, when I look at a 1016, I see history, I see Tenzing Norgay summiting Everest, whether that’s the actual truth or not. I am applying that to my perspective. And I’m also thinking about elegance in terms of what I like to wear. I’m thinking about how it sits on my wrist. I’m thinking about the simplicity in the design. And I can also see how someone else would appreciate the exact same thing about the Hublot: the work that went into skeletonizing that dial, the complication of a chronograph movement, and the mixture of metals and materials to make it. So I see both sides of it. I think because it is something so personal, it goes on your body. I think what ends up mattering is how you interpret that and whether you believe that one is of more value to you than the other stylistically.

Well, I think it sort of speaks to Harry’s world quite a bit. Harry comes from a world where if someone looked like they had money, they probably had money, right? And if they had nice shoes, they probably had a nice watch. And if they had a nice watch, they probably had money in their pocket. And you could do that math, and maybe it wouldn’t always be right, but these were educated guesses. And now we live in a world where a gold watch is not necessarily a gold watch. A Patek Philippe, presumably one of the most recognizable objects of value, is not necessarily an object of value. And to put that on Harry, to put that on a guy whose job it is to steal watches is, among other things, really a statement about him. And I guess in a wider sense that the world is not always what we think it is.

I think for the businessman at the beginning, he obviously has lots of nice suits and lots of nice shoes and he lives in a tall building on the Upper East Side and he’s got a camel hair coat and works in a fancy office. There are all these reasons to think that this guy is fancy and makes money. He doesn’t carry cash. You know what I mean? He wears Aldens, as we know, a fancy shoe, but he wears a fake watch. I think it speaks to where the world is right now, which is that it isn’t about honesty or dishonesty. There are shades of gray, and we exist in a bit of a gray world.

Great question. I think he knows that it’s fake. I think there is a world now where people—and I don’t think it’s just for watches, I think it’s for a lot of things—where people believe that getting most of the way toward something is enough. So somebody says to this guy, “Hey, you made partner. Isn’t it time to buy a $20,000 watch?” And then the guy next to him goes, “You can buy a $400 watch that looks just as good as a $20,000 watch.” And this guy goes, “Great.” And that’s it—that’s as far as they go.

“Too many” is the answer to how many watches I have. But most of what is in my collection that’s important to me are watches that are not [necessarily] of significant financial value. I have a watch that belonged to each of my grandfathers that I had restored. And I did not have fancy grandfathers. These are watches that cost more to restore than they were worth, but are of incredible value to me. And a couple of my friends who I’ve worked with many, many times, my friends and mentors in movies have given me watches, and those are important to me because of that, because of where they came from and what they mean and the consideration that went into them.

Watches like Benrus, which is, again, not a Rolex-level name, but Benjamin Lazarus founded that company in New York, and that means something to me as a guy from New York. So there’s something significant there. There are a lot of newer watches that I’m fascinated with, whether it’s companies like Oris or smaller brands like Haven or Bernhardt, which I appreciate.

I mean, listen, I don’t own an Omega Speedmaster. I’d love to own a Speedmaster. I love what they’re doing with modern watches now, actually. I’d love to own a gold Rolex. I think there’s something really cool about a gold Rolex.

I don’t know what I would do if I had a Rolex 6542, a Bakelite Bezel GMT [from the ’50s], because those are the coolest-looking watches. But if you sneeze at it wrong, does the bezel crack? I can’t worry about that.

Yeah, and I don’t believe in that! I want to wear my watches.

#6738. Presidents, Bullfighters, and California—Elaine de Kooning Painted Whatever She Wanted

And you can see it all at a new retrospective at Berry Campbell gallery in New York

In the history books, Elaine de Kooning is often eclipsed by her husband, the famed painter Willem. This fate befell the women in the Abstract Expressionist movement, including Lee Krasner, Grace Hartigan, Joan Mitchell, and Helen Frankenthaler, who became known as the “Ninth Street Women,” all of whom received their flowers after decades of being overshadowed by their male counterparts. But you simply cannot tell the story of mid-century art—and Abstract Expressionism—without Elaine.

De Kooning, who died in 1989 at 70, sat at the epicenter of the art world for five decades. She deftly balanced two parallel practices in portraiture and abstract expressionism, unafraid to allow these genres to intermingle. Beyond her painting, she founded the artist collective The Club in Greenwich Village and wrote art criticism for Art News, celebrating artists like Arshile Gorky and Jackson Pollock. President John F. Kennedy, New York artist Toni Ross, former Art News editor-in-chief Thomas Hess, and American painter Alex Katz are among the artist’s impressive roster of sitters. A number of these portraits currently hang at New York’s Berry Campbell gallery. Each image frames its subject with expressive brushwork and vivid, bright colors. Among these works, most featuring starry figures, is a young boy in a cowboy hat, featured in the painting Jemp #1 (1963). This little kid is De Kooning’s nephew, and the reason the show exists.

Gallerists Martha Campbell and Christine Berry connected with Chris Luyckx, the nephew, who had preserved De Kooning’s paintings for decades and felt her work deserved renewed attention. By the time they met, roughly a decade had passed since De Kooning’s last notable show, a retrospective at the National Portrait Gallery in 2015, followed by smaller shows that focused on specific periods of her life. “By doing these individual shows, you miss the incredible throughline of her work from the late 1940s until the day she died in 1989,” says Campbell. “It goes with our ethos of always believing in the artist from the very beginning until the very end.” Berry Campbell’s show, simply titled “Elaine De Kooning” and on view through December 19, celebrates the artist in her entirety, featuring around 30 works sourced directly from the family’s collection

De Kooning’s oeuvre retains its wonder by evading classification, collapsing boundaries between portraiture and abstract expressionism to forge a distinct visual sensibility. Part of her practice fit firmly in the world of abstract art. Paintings like Untitled (1960) reveled in obscuring the world around her; here, she depicts New York’s verticality. “Elaine de Kooning was an abstract expressionist, but as a woman artist, she didn’t have dealers breathing down her neck saying, ‘Paint more of what we see as Abstract Expressionism,” Campbell says, noting that this provided the artist with wiggle room.

This should not overshadow her exceptional command of pure abstraction. The 11-foot-wide California (1961), a barrage of vivid colors underscoring De Kooning’s compositional mastery, sits at the very back of the gallery. Berry affirms “it is the most important piece in the exhibition,” noting that “there is no other painting of that scale or magnitude or from that time period on the market, because very other painting that is like that is in a museum collection.” Doubling down on its consequence, Campbell recalls, “There’s a great note that we found from [legendary art dealer] Joan Washburn that says that when she was her dealer, she said, ‘This is the best painting that Elaine de Kooning has ever painted.’”

Elements of her abstract work often defined her portraiture. Energetic bursts of bright paint consumed her subjects. Tom Hess (1963), for instance, features the titular journalist among flurries of orange, yellow, and red paint, leaving most of the canvas untouched. “She was an abstract expressionist, but within her own definition of what that was, so she used these abstract expressionist brushstrokes to glorify what she loved.”

De Kooning loved her subjects, occasionally obsessing over one topic and painting it repeatedly, ranging from bullfighting and baseball to the painter Aristodimos Kaldis and President Kennedy. This new show highlights all of these hyperfocused periods, including a standout from her paintings of the former president. Her connection to him started in 1962, when Kennedy sat for De Kooning in Palm Beach to complete a commission for the Harry S. Truman Presidential Library & Museum. The fixation intensified after the president’s assassination in 1963. JFK #7 (1963), on view at the gallery, is only one example of a year’s worth of works.

“She did get fixated on JFK, because she was painting him and then he was shot,” Berry explains. “That was pretty shocking. She painted him for a full year without stopping. People only focus on JFK. But she did portraits from the beginning, in the 1940s, all the way through. She did self-portraits, as well as portraits of her neighbors and her boss, Tom Hess. The portraits are a through line of her career.”

A sophisticated command of color is evident across De Kooning’s entire body of work. Bright colors clash in her abstract works, and in her portraiture, color builds texture. Perhaps most surprising, however, is that De Kooning often avoided looking at color when creating her images. For instance, she preferred to use black-and-white newspaper clippings as references for her basketball paintings, imbuing them with color guided by her personal sensibility. “Color is key to what she does,” Berry explains, pointing to the portrait of poet Frank Lima, a friend with a drug problem whom De Kooning renders in muted greens.

One painting, Bacchus #20-G (1983), an image of Jules Dalou’s The Triumph of Silenus painted six years before her death, epitomizes what’s so striking about De Kooning’s paintings. The lush painting features the sculpture’s twisted bodies, rendered in an opulent violet, with a backdrop of verdant green. It demonstrates her capacity to seamlessly balance portraiture and Abstract Expressionism, a testament to her unwavering devotion to her distinct visual language. This vision, after years on the fringe, finally receives the flower it deserves, alongside, rather than below, her husband.

#6737. This Fashion Scion’s Laid-Back Ibiza Wedding Featured Lace Dresses, Barefoot Vows, and Dancing Till Dawn

It took the world grinding to a halt for Lola Teller, 29, and Freddie Woodruff, 35, to get going. A mutual friend had set them up on a date in 2020, but with Lola studying in Edinburgh and Freddie building his catering business, Noco, in London, geography got in the way. That is, until 12 months later, when lockdown found them separated by little more than a field in Boscastle, Cornwall, where Lola’s mother, fashion photographer and stylist Venetia Scott, owns a house, and Freddie was setting up a restaurant. “He used to come and cook for us every night, and a few weeks in, my mum was like, ‘Look, why don’t you come and live with us here?’” Lola says. “She was very fond of him, and I think she liked the food, so she was pushing.” What followed was an idyllic few months spent picking mussels on the beach and taking boats out into the Celtic Sea to catch lobsters. Eventually, though, it was time for Lola to begin her career in the art world—she is now director of the agenda-setting Bernheim gallery—and the couple moved in together in leafy north-west London. This time for good.

It was in July 2025 that Lola and Freddie got engaged, while staying at her family home on Hydra, where she has spent summers since childhood. “Fred decided he wanted to go on a hike at 4 p.m. in the boiling heat, and I was like, ‘This is ridiculous, no way,’” she says. “Something must be going on.” With nerves and temperatures running high, they barely spoke on the way up, and Freddie almost lost the ring—a trio of east-to-west oval Sophie Breitmeyer diamonds—among the rocks. “We got to the top of the mountain, completely dehydrated, just as the sun was setting, when he told me to sit on a rock and got down on one knee,” she recalls. “And it was really quite beautiful.” From there, the would-be-weds jetted off to Es Cucons, a family-run hotel in northern Ibiza, where the owners, who had been welcoming Lola and her mother for years, offered to host their wedding. “They said, ‘We don’t usually do this, but how does 40 guests sound?’, and we were like, ‘...150?’” They settled on 90, returning to the hotel at Christmas, Easter, and once more the following summer to finalize the plans.

There were even more visits—10 in total—to Kensington-based bridal designer Phillipa Lepley to perfect the lace wedding dress, complete with corset, veil, and train, and designed with the input of her mom. Having a mother behind some of Vogue’s most memorable covers must have come in handy? “Throughout the process, she was making me try on these enormous poofs of dresses, which looked great but were never gonna be the one for me,” Lola says. “Often I’d be like, ‘I like this!’, and then mum would be like, ‘...No.’ She’s always right, though.”

On the day, she paired the dress with white silk platform heels from “not a nice brand,” and diamond-and-pearl drop earrings borrowed from her stepmother’s collection. She would walk down the aisle flanked by her mom and dad, Juergen Teller, though despite having two of fashion’s most directional photographers at her fingertips, she still hired traditional wedding photographers to document the occasion. “Well, you want some of the classic shots,” she explains. “Plus, they wanted to enjoy themselves.” Indeed, Lola says Teller didn’t take “a single photo” throughout the weekend.

Which began with guests gathering for welcome cocktails among the fig and almond trees of the farmhouse hotel, before Lola, Freddie, and their closest family members headed to Chiringuito Cala Xuclar for an intimate dinner of grilled fish on the beach. “I think I had an hour of sleep that night,” Lola says, “which might have been because we were drinking quite late, but also… the nerves.” The morning of the wedding began with Lola kicking Freddie out of their room, before setting off on an hour-long coastal walk with her mum and bridesmaids. Saunas and ice baths followed, as they took their time getting ready for the ceremony. Once laced into her dress, Lola made her way up the hillside to a secluded grove, where her Armani-clad groom was waiting. Flanked by her parents, she walked down the aisle to Mazzy Star’s “Fade Into You,” though her entrance didn’t go entirely to plan. “It’s such a slow song, so it was really hard to time,” she says. “My veil got caught on a stone and nearly ripped my head off, which made it quite comical.” Following behind was a giddy procession of flower girls in La Coquetta dresses, among them her three-year-old sister, all walking at their own pace. “My 12-year-old goddaughter was sending me dresses that were, like, £500 each. Nice try.”

Lola’s uncle officiated the ceremony, which included a poem written by Freddie’s mother, a group singalong to Bob Marley’s “One Love,” and Lola tossing her bouquet as the newlyweds made their way back down the aisle. “I was ready for a drink at that point,” she says. “It was time.” The couple joined their loved ones in the hotel gardens for canapés of padrón peppers, octopus skewers, croquettes, and jamón, along with speeches and photographs, before everyone was ushered into a candlelit pergola for dinner, waving their napkins in the air to The Shapeshifters’ “Lola’s Theme.”

Dinner was served family-style: lamb chops, roast potatoes, and Spanish salads, before Lola steeled herself to make a speech of her own. “I was petrified, about to burst into tears,” she says. “But after a few drinks, it was fine, and I’m so glad I did it.” The room then erupted into an impromptu rendition of John Denver’s “Take Me Home, Country Roads,” giving Lola a chance to slip away and change into a beaded Clio Peppiatt minidress.

Back at the tables, a giant slab of tiramisu was wheeled in for the newlyweds to serve to their guests, who were in no hurry to move on. “I was like, ‘Guys, they’ve literally converted the yoga tent into a dance floor.’” DJ Fiona Jane played Ibiza bangers until 12:30 a.m., before the party spilled out around the swimming pool. “They were up till seven—the sign of a good wedding,” Lola says. “Freddie and I were asleep, luckily.”

The following morning was a slow one, with guests resurfacing in the afternoon for enormous pans of poolside paella—under mercifully cloudy skies, after days spent seeking refuge from the sun beneath parasols and behind fans—as friends of the couple took turns behind the decks. Lola wore a lace beach dress by Away That Day over a white bikini, before changing into a crochet Reformation number for one final hurrah at legendary nightlife institution Pikes. Well, the last official hurrah, anyway.

A handful of guests extended their stay, dropping in on the newlyweds at Atzaró Agroturismo Hotel—a 13-hectare farm-to-fork property where the tinkling of goats’ bells drifts over from neighboring farms and chickens roam freely—for a few days of decompression before Lola returned to London for the annual art-world frenzy that is Frieze. “A lot of people say that they come back and they have loads of wedding blues, but I just didn’t; I was just so happy that everything went so perfectly,” she says. “The whole thing was surreal, just the best feeling, heaven. I’ve spent every day since looking at the photos and trying to relive the happiest memories with our favorite people.”

Dancing into dinner to “Lola’s Theme” by The Shapeshifters.

#6736. All About Nicholas Hoult’s Wife, Bryana Holly

A month later, they made their red carpet debut at the Los Angeles premiere of Nosferatu, eight years after they first started dating.

Here’s everything to know about Bryana Holly and her connection to Hoult so far.

Holly is a model from California and she met Hoult in Los Angeles, per a 2019 interview the actor did with the Evening Standard. She primarily models lingerie and swimwear and is signed with Wilhelmina Models and No Ties Management. Holly was named Miss September by TransWorld Surf in 2012, according to Men’s Journal, when she was only 20 years old and living in Huntington Beach. In the interview, she described herself as a “mutt mix,” saying she has a diverse background of “Hawaiian, Japanese, Slovenian, Russian, and the list goes on.”

She also shared that her turn-ons include “Intelligence, good sense of humor, a man in a wetsuit,” and turnoffs are “cockiness, liars, and meatheads.”

In 2013, Holly dated Brody Jenner, brother to the famous Kardashian and Jenner sisters and star of The Hills.

In July 2022, Holly shared a carousel on Instagram titled “life lately” that included shots of Hoult.

In November 2024, while talking to E! News about watching Nosferatu with Holly, he said, “Afterwards, I remember I had my wife’s nails imprinted on my hand.”

The couple share one son, Joaquin, born in April 2018.

“He’s a great dad,” Davidson said. “Father of four. Four under 7.”

Hoult confirmed the news with a simple “Yeah.”

Davidson also praised Hoult for making time for his family while filming their movie, saying, “Elsie [Davidson’s ex and mother of his daughter] was pregnant while we were filming and he had just had his twins and he would fly back every weekend to go see his family and that was really awesome.”

#6735. A Definitive Guide to the Best Black Boots

Out of all the fall fashion purchases you make this season, there’s one item that is guaranteed to give you maximum mileage in the months ahead: a pair of black boots.

For those who favor a sleek silhouette to elevate and anchor your outfits, a classic knee-high boot complements dresses and skirts across the board. If you’d like your boots to serve as more of a personality piece, why not test drive a Western-inspired pair, or one detailed with moto hardware? Of course, timeless shapes like square-toe booties and Chelsea boots will always be reliable go-tos; trendier styles like the slouchy boot still feel just as versatile as they did decades ago.

Ahead, we break down nine different black boot styles, from equestrian-inspired riding boots to all-weather lug sole boots. Find the right one for you in our guide to the best black boots of the season.

A quintessential knee-high black boot can be worn layered beneath dresses and skirts or styled over slim trousers and denim. Let your personal preference inform the height—flat or block heels are best for commuters, while a higher heel can transition from the workday to evening seamlessly.

If you’re not yet a Western boot convert, the easiest way to style these silhouettes is to contrast them with wardrobe staples that don’t feel cowboy adjacent. Whether you’re letting your boots peek out from beneath a pair of wool trousers, or opting for a pair with subtler motifs, there’s always a way to make them feel your own.

Saint Laurent Dylan 45 Patent Leather Boots

A traditional Chelsea boot silhouette is the workhorse of many wardrobes. While a classic take on this style makes a great investment, don’t miss modern interpretations, like the Row’s, which are cut extra low.

Manolo Blahnik Chelsa Leather Chelsea Ankle Booties

Whether you’re going for moto-inspired hardware or something with a bit of downtown edge (Coach and Vince, as examples), a silver buckle is the kind of detail that adds dimension while staying versatile.

Manolo Blahnik Calica Buckled Biker Boots

For instant polish, slip into a pair of black riding boots. This equestrian-inspired silhouette is both classic and distinct, ideal with preppy separates like pleated skirts and boxy blazers.

The Row Nobilis Leather Knee-High Riding Boots

Khaite, Chloé, and several other designers included the slouchy boot in their fall 2026 collections, highlighting how this style has shifted away from its ’80s associations and in a much more compelling direction (particularly when rendered in classic black).

Preparing for the winter means being ready for the storms ahead, and a pair of lug-sole boots is a must. The season’s best styles offer all-weather protection (and are a stylish snow-boot alternative), while still feeling versatile enough to wear on glorious days when the weather is agreeable.

Not quite an ankle boot or a knee-high either—the mid-calf boot is shaping up to be one of the season’s most interesting shapes. Need proof? Just look to the designers embracing it—from cool-girl favorite Maryam Nassir Zadeh to buzzy newcomer Jude.

There’s a time and place for a pointed boot, but a sleek square toe always manages to feel a touch cooler. Look for styles with a slimmer, subtler square toe, so you can style them for any occasion.
